tips.title: Learn the definition word for word
tips.body: Cyber security is **the processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access**. It is quoted almost verbatim in mark schemes, so it is worth memorising.

tips.title: Seven threats, and one of them is people
tips.body: The list is: **Social engineering, Malicious code, Pharming, Weak and default passwords, Misconfigured access rights, Removable media, Unpatched and/or outdated software**. Notice that the first is about **people**, not technology — which is why it has a section of its own.

tips.title: Pharming redirects, phishing asks
tips.body: **Pharming** redirects a website's traffic to a **fake website** — the victim types the right address and still arrives at the wrong place. **Phishing** sends a message **asking** for details. One hijacks the route; the other asks nicely.

tips.title: A trojan is defined by disguise
tips.body: A **virus** spreads by attaching to files. A **trojan** does not spread itself — it **pretends to be something useful** so the user installs it willingly. The difference is how it gets in, not what it does afterwards.

tips.title: Two pen tests, two attackers
tips.body: Testing **with** knowledge or credentials simulates a **malicious insider**. Testing **without** any simulates an **external attack**. Say which attacker each one imitates and the mark is secured.

steps.title: What cyber security is
steps.body:
**The specification gives a definition worth learning exactly:**

> **Cyber security consists of the processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.**

Three things in that are worth noticing.

**It is not only technology.** **Processes** and **practices** — how an organisation works, what its staff are trained to do — sit alongside the technology. A company with excellent firewalls and untrained staff is not secure.

**It protects four things**: networks, computers, programs and data.

**Against three things**: attack, damage and unauthorised access. Note that **damage** need not be deliberate — an accidental deletion is a security failure too.

**The purposes of cyber security** are usually summarised as keeping data **confidential** (only those allowed can see it), **accurate** (nobody can alter it without authority), and **available** (those entitled to it can get at it when needed).

That last one is often forgotten. A system nobody can break into but nobody can use has also failed.

visuals.alt: A four-box card giving the definition of cyber security, what it protects, against what, and its purposes

check.prompt: According to the specification, what does cyber security consist of?
options: Processes, practices and technologies
Firewalls and antivirus software only
The laws governing computer misuse
Encryption applied to stored data
check.solution: **Processes, practices and technologies** designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data. Technology alone is not the whole of it — how people work matters just as much.

steps.title: The seven threats
steps.body:
**The specification lists seven threats you must be able to explain.**

**Social engineering techniques** — manipulating **people** into giving up confidential information. This is large enough to have its own section, covering blagging, phishing and shouldering.

**Malicious code (malware)** — hostile or intrusive software, covered in the next step.

**Pharming** — the specification's definition: **a cyber attack intended to redirect a website's traffic to a fake website**. The victim types the correct address and still lands somewhere false, where their details are captured.

**Weak and default passwords** — `password123`, or a router left on the factory password printed in its manual. Default passwords are published online, so a device that keeps one is effectively unlocked.

**Misconfigured access rights** — users able to reach data they should not. Often nobody attacks anything: the door was simply left open, and one careless or curious employee finds it.

**Removable media** — a USB stick carries malware **straight past the firewall**, because it never travels over the network at all.

**Unpatched and/or outdated software** — a known flaw left unfixed. Once a patch is published, the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**, so unpatched machines become **easier** to attack, not harder.

**Notice how many involve no clever technology.** Weak passwords, misconfigured rights and unpatched software are all failures of **process**, which is exactly why the definition mentions processes and practices.

known flaws left unfixed because updates were not applied

check.prompt: Which threat is defined as an attack intended to redirect a website's traffic to a fake website?
check.solution: **Pharming.** The victim enters the correct address but is sent to a fake site, where their details are captured.

steps.title: Malware
steps.body:
**Malware is an umbrella term** used to refer to a variety of forms of **hostile or intrusive software**. The specification names three forms.

**Virus** — attaches itself to a **file**, and spreads when that file is **opened** or shared. It needs the file to travel and the user to run it.

**Trojan** — **disguises itself as something useful** so that the user **installs it willingly**. Named after the wooden horse: the defences are not broken, they are **walked through**. A trojan does **not** spread itself.

**Spyware** — **secretly records what the user does**, such as the keys they press, and sends it back to the attacker. Passwords and card numbers are captured as they are typed, so encryption of the stored data does not help.

**The difference between them is how they get in and spread**, not what they do afterwards. Any of the three might steal data or damage files. A virus **attaches**, a trojan **deceives**, spyware **watches**.

**Protecting against malware:** anti-malware software, a **firewall**, **keeping software up to date**, not opening attachments or installing programs from unknown sources, and **restricting who may install software** at all.

**Backups** belong on that list too. They do not prevent an infection, but they mean a successful one does not have to be a disaster.

check.prompt: What distinguishes a trojan from a virus?
options: It is disguised as something useful so the user installs it
It damages files rather than stealing information
It spreads automatically to every computer on a network
It can only infect a computer through removable media
check.solution: A **trojan** pretends to be something the user **wants**, so they install it themselves — the defences are walked through rather than broken. A **virus** attaches to a file and spreads when that file is opened.

steps.title: Penetration testing
steps.body: **The specification defines penetration testing as the process of attempting to gain access to resources without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access.** In short: attacking your own system on purpose to find the holes before someone else does.

visuals.problem: Explain what penetration testing is and describe the two types.

steps.text: It is an **authorised** attempt to break into a system, to find weaknesses **before a real attacker does**
steps.note: authorised is the word that separates it from a crime

steps.text: The point is to find what is **actually** exploitable, rather than what is believed to be secure
steps.note: a system is only as secure as its weakest point, which is rarely the one people worry about

steps.text: **First type:** the tester has **with knowledge and possibly basic credentials**
That answers: how much damage could someone **already inside** do — an employee, or an attacker who has stolen one password?
steps.note: it tests what lies behind the front door, where access rights are often misconfigured

steps.text: **Second type:** the tester has **with no knowledge of any credentials**
That answers: could a stranger with no help get in at all?
steps.note: it tests the front door itself

steps.text: Both are needed, because they test **different** things
steps.note: a strong front door proves nothing about what an insider could reach

with no knowledge of any credentials

check.prompt: A penetration tester is given no credentials at all. Which attacker does this simulate?
options: An external attack
A malicious insider
An accidental data loss
A hardware failure
check.solution: With **no knowledge of any credentials**, the test simulates an **external attack** — a stranger trying to get in. Testing **with** knowledge or basic credentials simulates a **malicious insider**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Quote the definition.** *Processes, practices and technologies designed to protect networks, computers, programs and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.* Mark schemes follow this wording closely, and the **processes and practices** half is the part students leave out.

**Keep pharming and phishing apart.** **Pharming redirects** traffic to a **fake website**; **phishing asks** by message. The reason pharming is more dangerous is worth stating: the victim **types the correct address** and has no reason to be suspicious, because nothing they can see is wrong.

**Explain the patch paradox.** When a patch is published, the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**. Attackers read the patch to learn what was wrong, so an unpatched machine is **more** exposed after the fix exists than before. That is why "we'll update it later" is worse than it sounds.

**Say why removable media defeats a firewall.** A firewall inspects traffic **crossing the network boundary**. A USB stick carries data **physically past** it, so the file never comes under inspection at all. Naming the mechanism earns more than naming the threat.

**Define a trojan by disguise, not by damage.** A trojan **pretends to be useful** so the user installs it willingly — the defences are **walked through**, not broken. It does **not** spread itself, which is the clearest difference from a virus.

**Explain spyware's specific danger.** It captures information **as it is typed**, so encrypting stored data protects nothing — the password is taken **before** any encryption happens.

**Match each penetration test to its attacker.** With knowledge or basic credentials → a **malicious insider**. With none → an **external attack**. Add why both are run: a secure front door says nothing about what someone already inside could reach.

**Notice how many threats are not attacks.** Weak and default passwords, misconfigured access rights and unpatched software are failures of **process**. No attacker was clever; a door was left open. Making that observation shows you have understood why the definition mentions processes at all.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Cyber security** is the **processes, practices and technologies** designed to protect **networks, computers, programs and data** from **attack, damage or unauthorised access**.
- It aims to keep data **confidential**, **accurate** and **available**.
- The seven threats: **Social engineering techniques**, **Malicious code (malware)**, **Pharming**, **Weak and default passwords**, **Misconfigured access rights**, **Removable media**, **Unpatched and/or outdated software**.
- **Pharming** redirects a website's traffic to a **fake website**.
- **Phishing asks**; **pharming redirects** — the victim types the right address.
- **Default passwords** are published online, so an unchanged one is no protection.
- **Misconfigured access rights** let users reach data they should not.
- **Removable media** carries malware **physically past the firewall**.
- **Unpatched software** is **more** exposed after a patch, because the flaw becomes public.
- **Malware** is an umbrella term for **hostile or intrusive software**.
- A **virus** attaches to a file and spreads when it is opened.
- A **trojan** is **disguised as something useful**, and does not spread itself.
- **Spyware** records what the user does, such as keys pressed.
- **Penetration testing** is attempting to gain access **without** the normal means of access.
- **With** credentials it simulates a **malicious insider**; **without**, an **external attack**.

questions.prompt: Explain what malware is, describe the three forms named in the specification, and explain how a system can be protected against it.
questions.solution:
**Malware** is an **umbrella term** used to refer to a variety of forms of **hostile or intrusive software**. It is not one thing but a category, and the specification names three forms.

A **virus attaches itself to a file** and spreads when that file is **opened** or shared. It needs a host file to travel in and a user to run it, and it may then damage or delete data as well as spreading further.

A **trojan disguises itself as something useful** — a game, a utility, an attachment that appears legitimate — so that the user **installs it willingly**. It is named after the wooden horse for good reason: the defences are not broken, they are **walked through**. Unlike a virus, a trojan does **not** spread itself; it relies entirely on persuading each user in turn.

**Spyware secretly records what the user does**, typically the **keys they press**, and sends that information back to the attacker. Passwords, card numbers and messages are all captured as they are typed.

**The three are distinguished by how they get in and spread**, not by the damage they do. A virus **attaches**, a trojan **deceives**, and spyware **watches**. Any of them might be used to steal data or to damage files once installed.

**Protection** works at several points. **Anti-malware software** scans files and running programs against known threats and behaviour, catching infections that are already recognised. A **firewall** monitors incoming and outgoing traffic and blocks what its rules do not permit. **Keeping software up to date** closes known flaws — and matters more than it sounds, because once a patch is published the flaw it fixes becomes **public knowledge**, leaving unpatched machines more exposed than before.

Other measures target the way malware actually arrives. **Not opening attachments or installing software from unknown sources** addresses the trojan directly, since a trojan cannot install itself. **Restricting who may install software** limits the damage a single careless user can do. Controlling the use of **removable media** matters because a USB stick carries files **physically past the firewall**, which never inspects them.

**Backups** belong on the list as well. They prevent nothing, but they mean a successful attack — particularly one that destroys or encrypts data — need not be a disaster.

Note that against **spyware** specifically, encrypting stored passwords does not help: the keystrokes are captured **as they are typed**, before anything is stored, so the protection is applied at the wrong point in the chain.

Describes spyware and distinguishes the three clearly.
Explains protective measures and why they work.

questions.prompt: A company suffers a data breach. Explain the threats that could have caused it and describe how penetration testing could have helped prevent it.
questions.solution:
Several of the threats in the specification could account for a breach, and they are worth separating into **attacks** and **failures of process**.

Among the **attacks**: **social engineering** could have persuaded an employee to hand over their login, since manipulating a person needs no technical weakness at all. **Malware** — a **trojan** disguised as a useful program, or **spyware** capturing passwords as they were typed — could have given the attacker credentials. **Pharming** could have redirected staff to a fake version of a login page, where the victim would type the **correct** address and still surrender their details.

Among the **failures of process**: **weak or default passwords** may simply have been guessed, and default passwords are **published online**, so an unchanged one is effectively no password. **Misconfigured access rights** might have meant an ordinary employee could already reach data they had no business seeing, in which case no attack was needed. **Unpatched software** could have left a known flaw open — and once a patch exists the flaw becomes **public knowledge**, so delay makes a system **more** exposed, not less. **Removable media** could have carried malware **physically past the firewall**, which never inspects a file that does not cross the network.

**Penetration testing** is the **authorised** process of attempting to gain access to resources **without knowledge of usernames, passwords and other normal means of access** — attacking your own system deliberately to find what is genuinely exploitable, rather than what is assumed to be safe.

The specification describes **two types**. In the first, the tester has **knowledge of the system and possibly basic credentials**, simulating **a malicious insider**. In the second, the tester has **no knowledge of any credentials**, simulating an **external attack**.

**How testing would have helped** depends on which weakness was exploited, which is exactly why both types are run. An **external** test would have tried to get in from outside with nothing to start from, and would likely have found **default passwords** on exposed devices and **unpatched software** with known public flaws. An **insider** test, starting from an ordinary employee account, would have revealed **misconfigured access rights** — showing how far a single compromised login could actually reach.

The insider test is the one organisations most often skip, and it is the one that matters most here. A company can have an impeccable front door and still lose everything if one stolen password opens the whole building. Testing only from outside would have confirmed the perimeter was strong while leaving that entirely unexamined.

It is worth being honest about the limits, though. Penetration testing finds **technical** weaknesses well, but the threat it addresses least directly is **social engineering**, because that attacks **people** rather than systems. A company relying on pen testing alone would still need **staff training**, which is precisely why the definition of cyber security names **processes and practices** alongside technologies.

examTechnique.body:
Quote the definition, including **processes and practices**, not technologies alone. Keep **pharming** (redirects to a fake site) apart from **phishing** (asks by message).

Define a **trojan** by its **disguise**, not its damage. Match each penetration test to the attacker it simulates: **with** credentials is an **insider**, **without** is **external**.
examinerErrors: Defining cyber security as technology alone.
Describing a trojan by what it damages rather than its disguise.
Saying a trojan spreads itself like a virus.
Naming removable media without saying it bypasses the firewall.
Missing that a published patch makes the flaw public.
Describing only one type of penetration testing.
Forgetting that penetration testing must be authorised.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes the definition with **processes, practices and technologies**, and notices that several listed threats — weak passwords, misconfigured rights, unpatched software — are **failures of process** rather than clever attacks. It separates **pharming** from **phishing** by saying the victim **types the correct address**, defines a **trojan** by **disguise** and notes it does **not** spread itself, and explains why encryption cannot stop **spyware** (the keystroke is captured **before** anything is stored). On penetration testing it names **both** types with the attacker each simulates, says why both are needed, and concedes what testing cannot find: **social engineering**, which attacks people rather than systems.
